What you have learned of Maresh, and the records you have found on the way.
What the islands believe, and what they have lived through.
The shores, roads and temples walked so far.
Words left in the world by other hands: notices, notes and inscriptions.

When a lamp goes out, it breaks into motes of light. Most of them lift toward the stars within a night and are gone. Some sink instead and drift seaward, cool and blue, and divers who meet that light underwater leave it be. The Order forbids binding glimmer into anything.

Once a generation a storm rises that does not move like weather. It wanders the sea as if it were looking for something, and it drowns whole coasts. For days afterward the water glows with the dead it leaves behind. The Order of the Still Water teaches that it is the price of the old binding, and that one day the price will be paid.

Each temple of the Order keeps a Saint: a Cantor of an earlier generation whose light stayed, the Order says, to teach the ones who come after. A Cantor who passes a temple's trial learns a verse of the Hush there and may call on its Saint from then on. The Shell Shrine's is Ilun, a great ray of netted light. When Asha calls him, the others step back and he stands in their place.

A fishing village in the Low Reaches, built of coral stone, with walls of set shells and roofs like opened fans. Carved gulls on the roof ridges watch the sea for weather. When the dead come in on the tide, its people go down to the beach to meet them, so that no one comes ashore alone.

A tidal road of saltgrass and coral boulders between Haluna and the Shell Shrine's islet. It opens this far only at the lowest tides, twice a month, on days the Order's tide-readers set. Reef crabs and lantern-lure eels keep to its pools, and old timber posts mark the line for anyone the turning tide catches.

Haluna's small temple of Water, on a tidal islet at the causeway's end. Its halls hold great shell-basins that turn to send the water where it is asked to go, until the inner pool fills and the chamber door floods open. It is tended and swept and loved, and it is the first temple on the road from Haluna.

A girl of Haluna who found Rhen in the shallows at dawn and smiled before she said a word. She woke her house before light that morning so the drowned would not come ashore alone, though no one had told her they were coming. The whole village treats her with a care that seems too gentle for an ordinary day.

Asha's guardian, who carries a long spear and the manners of a temple. He answers greetings with the Order's words before he has thought about them, and he weighs everything else he says as if it costs him. He watches Asha the way a man watches a lamp in the wind.

Nailed to a causeway post, the ink run by salt: "The road to the Shell Shrine stands open from the second hour after the low until the turn. Walk in company. Do not linger at the pools when the water begins to talk. If the tide takes the path, climb the nearest post and wait; the sea has always given this road back."

Cut into the first step of the shrine, worn smooth by knees: "Water does not hurry, and it is never late. Turn the shells gently and it will go where you ask. Leave the basins as you found them, for whoever comes after you."

Oruvel's divers go down weighted into the drowned towers of the Lit Age, with an oil lantern and a tether, and walk the floors instead of swimming them. They cut out old brass and glass and sell it by the pound to whoever pays, and the Order's scale-man stamps each lot unbound. Pockets of trapped air, the bell-rooms, let a diver breathe between floors. The oldest rule of the trade is that nobody goes below the ninth floor.
The Order of the Still Water

The faith of Maresh, whose sign is the Level: a circle crossed by one line of still water. It teaches that the Lit Age bound the dead and the sea rose to collect the debt, and that stillness is the atonement: build nothing that binds, keep no lamps but oil, mourn quietly and send the dead to the sea. Its people greet each other with "Be level" and answer "And still". Tenders keep its temples, and the Stillguard, in red-lacquered shell armour, keep its law.

The night before a Cantor leaves on pilgrimage, her village holds her funeral while she is alive to attend it. There is food, and there are songs, and her name is carved on a shell and set in the shrine wall beside the names of the Cantors who went before her. In Haluna the people carry their lamps out to the wall and leave their windows dark behind them.

A people descended from engineers who refused the Salt Edicts, and who wear the old insult in their name with pride. They live in flotillas of lashed hulls and put to work what the Lit Age bound, because, they say, the dead want to be useful. Each fine line tattooed on a wright's arm records a device the wright has restored. Their chalk sign, a circle with fine parallel lines, means that wrights work here, and the Order hunts them for it.

The drowned Lit Age towers under Oruvel, where the raft-town's lamp-divers work. The floors are coral-crusted concrete, and the galleries are rows of dead lamp-columns, white ceramic gone green, empty for four hundred years. Bell-rooms of trapped air hold a diver's breath between floors. A knotted cord across the stairwell says what every diver knows: nobody goes below the ninth floor.

A raft-town of lashed hulls in every colour the sun has faded, moored over a drowned Lit Age district in the Low Reaches. Its people are lamp-divers, poor and loud and fond of each other, and its plank bridges run between the scale-hull, the cookboats, the net lanes and the old keel-hull where the town meets. Carved gulls on every roof ridge face the sea; they are said to cry before the Undertow.

A two-masted Low Reaches ferry, hired by the Order to carry the Cantor from Haluna's islet to Pemakar for Lanternfall. She has a deckhouse with a small Order shrine, an awning for her passengers and a skiff on her davits. Her ferry-master, Imbe, keeps the old sea-law, and on this crossing she carries terrace traders, a Reed going home and a child too shy to look at the Cantor.

A terraced town on the flank of a volcano, its tiers cut into rice paddies, market terraces, smithies and lacquer workshops. Its gates are stone forearms with open hands, and its graves sit beside the paddies, so its festivals are held among the dead. At Lanternfall every household floats leaf-boats down the terrace channels until the whole mountain runs with small fires. The plume's thunder, they say, is Daro's hammer.

The temple of Lightning, a stair-mountain built into the lip of a caldera that still breathes ash. Old Lit Age copper veins its tiers, so the strikes run down the mountain like water down the terraces. Pilgrims climb past the Tenders' gate and the grave tier to a red-lacquered pavilion at the crown, where dry storms crackle in the plume.

Low water over a drowned country: grey-green silted flats, ridges of black Lit Age hull plating and wooden hulks, and tide-channels between them that fill faster than they look. Gulls work the wrecks at every hour. Saltwright chalk marks show where the wrights have been, and by law everything on the shoals is under the Edict.

A stilt city at a river mouth, with gilded lacquer signboards on every house-front, markets that float hull to hull, and a hundred languages. Above it hangs the Tamsule Bell, a dome of the Lit Age with a drop of seawater held in its mouth, lit from within. In Tidecup week the whole coast comes to watch the Reefball sides play, and every purse-cutter on the coast comes with it.

The stilt galleries inside the Bell's gantry, tier on tier around the catch-pool where Tidecup is played. The drop hangs above them, perfectly still. Each side has its moorings under the Bell's skirt, iron rings set in a timber staging, and its people watch from the galleries over them.

A town that lives behind a seawall of grey laterite blocks carved with rows of faces, the Watchers, their eyes closed and their mouths open. The Fisher Stair is cut up the wall's inner face. The fishers of its stair-watch keep one law: first down the stair, last up it.

Oruvel's chandler, who has sold the lamp-divers their oil and trimmed their wicks for forty years from a hull she will not step off. She never learned to swim. She took Rhen in when he was eight and nobody came for him, the way she took in every stray the raft-town had, and she gives every diver a wick before they go down. "For luck."
Asha's aunt, who mends nets and pretends not to be afraid. She feeds Rhen the way she would talk to a stray dog she has decided to keep: often, and far too much.

A scholar of Lamptongue from Ansedra, appointed by the Order to tutor the Cantor on her pilgrimage. She came aboard at the islet's landing with the Order's letter and very little else to say. She is exacting, correct and witheringly polite, and she keeps a step apart from everyone.

A silent, scarred swordsman who caught a child out of the weir at Pemakar and stayed with the party after. He says almost nothing, least of all about himself, and he swings a blade heavy enough to break armour.

A smith of Pemakar's forge lane, in his sixties, with burn-scarred forearms and a big, careful voice. He can true a blade to a hair and makes a ruin of folding a leaf-boat. His son went to Oruvel to learn to dive.

A Saltwright mechanic from the Hollowmere flotilla, quick and sharp with everyone. She was running a salvage camp on the Brine Shoals when the Order burned it, and she came away with one crate of parts and a grudge that could float a ship. Toma's Stillguard papers get her past the checkpoints, which is the reason she gives for staying.

The High Warden, head of the Order of the Still Water, met on the Brine Shoals on his once-a-Calm progress along the coast. His white barge leaves no wake. He is warm and witty, and humble in a way nobody on the coast expects of the head of their faith.

Mother Kell's grandson, captain of Oruvel's Reefball side in its oil-black and brass. He and Rhen grew up around the same stall on the second mooring. They are not brothers, but they had the same person.

A Kirru, far taller than a man, long-necked, with an otter's face and a crest of fine heron feathers. The name-shell at his throat has been scraped blank. He came down to the strand at Corrow on the night of the Ebbing, watched it a long while, and called it beautiful.

The temple of Fire, a hollow stone spire on the headland beyond Corrow's wall-gate, with copper flue-pipes coiled up its outside like vines. Its Tenders keep a flame that a Cantor must walk up the flues, tier by tier, to the crown. From the beacon gallery at the top you can see out to where the storms always break.

A Stillguard of Corrow's wall, Toma's shield-mate for seven years. He hugged Toma hard enough to lift him off the wall-head, knelt properly to the Cantor, and took to Rhen at once. Toma laughed out loud when he saw him.
